## The problem, in one picture {.smaller}

![](figures/circularity.dot){width=88%}

The legacy build fetched `VIEWS` **from bioconductor.org**, converted it to
`packages.json`, and rendered ~92,000 package pages from it.

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
Any migration plan that begins *"first, stand up the new site"* immediately
discovers it cannot — because the new site's data source is the old site.
:::

---

## What that circle costs us

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**The estate it holds in place**

- Mac, Linux, Windows builders — three **purchased, physically maintained** boxes
- Master webserver
- Staging webserver
- CloudFront + S3 bucket
- Open Storage Network buckets for public assets
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**The bill**

[$5k]{style="font-size:3.4em; font-weight:700; line-height:1.15; display:block;"}

per month, AWS alone — **~$60k/year**

Before builder hardware, refresh cycles, or the staff time to keep three
operating systems patched and building.
:::
:::

---

## The knot

> The builders could not be retired without the website moving.
>
> The website could not move without a non-circular data source.

. . .

So nothing could be retired **individually** — the estate was jointly
load-bearing, and the website was the thing holding it together.

. . .

**Untying that knot is what this work does.**

# What we built

---

## Two halves, one seam

![](figures/seam.noml){width=95%}

Nothing downstream of the contract knows where the data came from.
Nothing upstream knows how it is rendered.

::: {.fragment}
That seam is why the **same component** renders both the legacy-parity pages
and the new `/next/` pages, unchanged.
:::

---

## Where the data comes from now {.smaller}

![](figures/origins.dot){width=93%}

Every source is a **genuine origin** — the place the data is actually authored
— and none of them is a machine we are trying to switch off.

---

## Origins, measured {.smaller}

![](figures/origins-chart.vl.json){width=78%}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**3,772 of 3,804 packages** in release 3.23 now come from a real origin.
The 32 that don't are named in `provenance.json`, not papered over.
:::

---

## How annotation packages got a real origin

r-universe covers Bioconductor **software** only. The other ~1,390 packages had
no origin outside the site being rebuilt.

. . .

`DESCRIPTION` inside the source tarball **is** the real origin — the
maintainer's own file. But downloading 1,392 tarballs means hundreds of
gigabytes to read a few hundred bytes each.

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
**The trick:** `DESCRIPTION` sits near the front of the archive, gzip is a
stream, and object stores serve ranged requests. Fetch the **first 64 KB**,
inflate what that yields, walk the tar headers.

**~0.1–0.2 s per package, bounded at 64 KB regardless of package size.**
:::

. . .

Whole-archive facts the prefix cannot see are reported as **unavailable**,
never guessed — guessing them `false` would silently drop documentation links
from ~1,400 pages.

---

## Correctness is measured, not asserted {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Precision
Every URL we emit must exist upstream.

*Inventing a URL is worse than omitting one — a 200 on a page the real site
does not have is a silent wrong answer.*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Recall
Every URL upstream has must be emitted — reported **per page type**.

*One number over a corpus that is 99% package pages would read as ~100% while
every prose page was missing.*
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Release 3.23, diffed path-by-path against the legacy build:
**7,614 identical paths. Zero spurious.**
:::

---

## What it produces today {.smaller}

| | |
|---|---|
| Package landing pages | **35 releases** (2.5–3.24), ~92,000 |
| Page count vs. record count | **exact match**, everywhere |
| Prose | 535 pages + 171 events, **~97%** resolved |
| Full build | **~97,000 pages in ~60 seconds** |
| Machines needed to build it | **one** — and no database |
| Code | ~1,300 lines Python + ~2,000 Astro |
| Runtime dependencies | **4** |
| Search | build-time index, **no backend** |

# How it ships

---

## Publish, then decide what to serve

![](figures/publish.dot){width=92%}

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
**This repo publishes builds. The Worker decides what is served.**
Write access to the site repo never implies the power to change production.
:::

---

## No flag day

The Worker serves **mirrored legacy content** for everything not yet ported.

. . .

Routes flip to new builds **one surface at a time**.

. . .

Every flip is reversible in seconds — deploy is a pointer move, rollback is
moving the pointer back.

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
This is the *strangler* pattern. There is no cutover weekend, and no moment
where the project is betting on a single switch.
:::

---

# Three projects, one estate

---

## Which repo retires which machine {.smaller}

![](figures/division.dot){width=100%}

**Define where the data comes from once, and let every consumer render it.**
The website is one consumer — deliberately *not* the place where "what is true
about a package" gets decided.

---

## bioc-registry: the connective tissue {.smaller}

![](figures/registry.dot){width=92%}

---

## The repository is the point

The old builders did not just build packages.

. . .

They produced **the repository** — `src/contrib`, `PACKAGES`, the thing
`install.packages()` actually reads.

. . .

```r
install.packages("edgeR",
  repos = "https://bioc-registry.seandavi.workers.dev/repo/bioc")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
A data plane that emits an installable repository is what makes the builders
**removable**, rather than merely unfashionable. This works today.
:::

---

## The estate, mapped {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
![](figures/estate.dot){width=100%}
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
<br>

- **Staging webserver** — already redundant. Per-PR previews are strictly
  better: one per change, isolated, identical to production output.

- **Master** — its role as a *data source* is gone. What remains is serving
  bytes. With staging, **about half the AWS bill.**

- **CloudFront + S3** — like-for-like replacement, **no egress billing**.

- **OSN buckets** — public assets on best-effort academic storage is exposure
  with no upside. This is a storage swap, not a migration.
:::
:::

---

## Where the $60k goes {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### ~half — master + staging

Substantial machines. Pure compute, for a workload that no longer needs a
server at all.

**A static build has no origin to run.** This is the half the website work
retires directly.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### ~half — CloudFront + S3

A package repository is **almost entirely egress** — "serve tarballs and static
pages to the world" is the shape CloudFront bills most aggressively for.

**R2 charges no egress fees.**
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The whole line is in scope — split about evenly between **two machines that stop
existing** and **egress that stops being billed**. Storage is modest either way:
the entire 35-release corpus is 175 MB.
:::

---

# What this opens up

---

## Check results as a first-class page

The legacy site **never built check pages.**

. . .

- `/next/{universe}/checkResults.html` — the check matrix, worst-first, with a
  propagated-version column
- `/next/{universe}/package/{pkg}.html` — a landing page per propagated package

. . .

Rendered through the **same component** as the parity pages.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Version truth is the **propagation index** — not "whatever r-universe last
built". Where the two disagree, the page says so in a banner rather than
hiding it.
:::

---

## Finding packages, and finding anything

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Package finder**

One box matching names, titles, and category terms. Category tree as facet
navigation, results as a table.

The legacy `#___Term` deep-link contract still works.

*Deliberately the site's only hydrated island.*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Site-wide search**

A build-time index. No search service to run, fund, or monitor.

*The legacy site's search needed a backend. This one needs a file.*
:::
:::

---

## The site becomes contributable

Today, the number of people who can safely change bioconductor.org is bounded
by who has access to the build host and knows nanoc, ERB, and Haml.

. . .

Under this model: **fork, edit, PR, preview URL, merge.**

. . .

Every pull request gets a preview that is byte-for-byte what production would
serve — reviewable by anyone, requiring access to nothing.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The same workflow the community already uses for packages.
:::

---

## Questions we could not previously ask {.smaller}

The logging built to keep download ranks alive lands something bigger: request
logs that are **structured, queryable, and accumulating over time.**

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
### User journeys
How do people actually move through the site? Where do they enter, and where
do they give up?
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Hot vs. unused
Which of ~97,000 pages carry the traffic? Which prose pages have not been read
in a year?
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Change over time
The same questions across releases — so a redesign's effect is **observed**,
not argued about.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
A daily job that emits a rank table cannot express any of these. A site with a
measured usage distribution can be pruned and reorganised **on evidence**.
:::

---

## Degradation as a property, not a hope

- An r-universe outage degrades `/next/` pages to *"no download counts"* — it
  never fails a build
- Code highlighting happens at build time, so no page depends on a CDN being up
  to render
- jQuery is served from the vendored copy, not a 2011 Google CDN URL — one
  fewer third-party origin

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
`just install && just data && just build` — no credentials, no build host, no
database. Anyone can run the whole thing.
:::

---

# What is not closed

---

## The annotation / experiment / workflow path {.smaller}

Eliminating the builders is the plan. r-universe closes it for **software**.
It does not cover the other three repositories — ~1,390 packages, a third of
the corpus.

. . .

**This is the last thing standing between the estate and three fewer machines.**

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
The useful news: **the website does not constrain the answer.** Those pages
already read `DESCRIPTION` from the tarballs, from a mirror.

The site imposes exactly one requirement:

> **the tarballs must be reachable over HTTP with ranged reads**

Anything satisfying that keeps ~1,390 landing pages building unchanged — and
bioc-registry's artifact store already provides it for software.
:::

---

## Web stats: the input is already replaced {.smaller}

The worrying version of this — *"turn off CloudFront and download ranks stop"* —
**no longer applies.**

. . .

The new site already logs through the Worker to a **GCP bucket**, in the **same
format as the CloudFront logs**. GCP for privacy control and BigQuery access.
Capture is running today.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
What remains is porting the Flask/Postgres service that turns those logs into
`Rank`. **Ordinary work, not a blocker** — on the list because it isn't done,
not because it's hard.

`bio-web-stats` is only *addressed* through the shared hostname — that route is
a **must-preserve** item at cutover.
:::

## The one-slide version {.smaller}

::: {.r-fit-text}
The website was the knot.
:::

<br>

- It is untied: **no page is built from data the retiring machines produce**
- Reproduction is **measured** — 7,614 identical paths, zero spurious
- Serving is a pointer move, so the migration has **no flag day**
- The staging box is **already** redundant; master, CloudFront, S3 and the OSN
  buckets have ready replacements
- **~$60k/year** of AWS is in scope — about half of it master and staging alone
  — before hardware and staff time

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
What remains between here and three fewer machines is a **package
infrastructure** question — where annotation, experiment, and workflow packages
get built — not a website one.
:::
